what_it_does: Designing a printed circuit board (PCB) means placing hundreds of physical components — chips, capacitors, connectors — on a board so that they do not collide, meet electrical spacing rules, and leave room for routing copper wires between them. The task is hard because modern boards mix components with irregular, non-rectangular shapes, and the design-rule constraints multiply quickly. This paper describes a three-stage automated placement pipeline: a global stage that detects collisions using the Separating Axis Theorem (a geometry test that checks whether two arbitrary shapes overlap by projecting them onto candidate axes), a force-directed refinement stage that pushes components apart or together like springs to balance clearance and wire-routability, and a final legalization stage that scans the board and resolves any remaining overlaps while enforcing spacing rules. Together, the three stages handle arbitrarily shaped components and complex design constraints without human intervention, according to the abstract.
